newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts see no hurry for Swedish bank merger.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see no hurry for Swedish bank merger.

text.p: Shares in Swedish banking groups Nordbanken and S-E-Banken have rallied on speculation about a merger but analysts are not so sure a deal will be be struck in the near future.
"I do not believe that a merger is unlikely but I lean toward the view that it will not happen," Fredrik Myren, analyst at HSBC James Capel in Stockholm, told Reuters.
Other analysts are divided, talking about a 50-50 chance of a merger, while some are cautiously positive.
"A merger seems logical," Goran Kallebo at Matteus brokerage said.
But, while a recent newspaper article speculated on a quick deal, analysts do not believe that the banks will act before the New Year as they have no need to be in such a hurry.

Despite noting several reasons for a merger, such as the fact that the banks would complement each other, they point to difficulties that could obstruct a link -- for example that the banks have different cultures and complicated ownership.
But investors' mouths are watering at the thought of a merger, which is likely to push the merged bank's shares up by between 20 and 25 percent, according to analysts.

In the past week, Nordbanken's shares have soared 7.6 percent to 197.5 crowns, while S-E-Banken's shares have risen 6.3 percent to 67 crowns. Both have been outperforming a general index advance of 3.3 percent.
A merger would create a huge bank able to compete with other large European banks which are expected to enter the Swedish market after European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is launched in 1999.

The banks would also be complementary. Nordbanken is currently focusing on private customers, small companies and municipalities, while S-E-Banken has its strength in large company deals and investment banking.

On the other hand, this means that the banks have different cultures with S-E-Banken being more of a risk-taker and operating with lower margins in more competitive market segments, while Nordbanken is more of a traditional bank with higher margins.
"It is not sure that Nordbanken is overjoyed about a merger as it has the highest return on equity of all Swedish banks," Myren said.
The different images, with S-E-Banken as the corporate bank and Nordbanken as the bank for the average Swede, could also prompt customers to depart in case of a merger, analysts said.

"An S-E-Banken customer might not want to enter a Nordbanken office and a Nordbanken customer might not, for ideological reasons, want to turn to an S-E-Banken office," said Jonny Sylven, analyst at banking group Swedbank.
Ownership is also a problem as the state holds 59 percent in Nordbanken, although it intends to sell its stake, while the Wallenberg family and its associates own around 15 percent in S-E-Banken.

Analysts said the Wallenbergs, Sweden's best-known industrialists, were probably not keen on the state controlling their bank, while the state was probably not interested in acquiring new banking shares.

As neither bank is strong enough to make a cash takeover bid for the other, analysts expect that in case of a merger, they would agree a share deal and somehow pay the state in cash, for instance through a new share issue.
